views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the May 19 framework alive and send teams to work agriculture and energy purchase details with Ross, but do not lock a $200 billion deficit-cut number or open Made in China 2025. Use those purchase talks to pin down ZTE relief and keep the Section 301 list on ice. Leave the existing $3 billion Section 232 retaliation in place as residual leverage; do not add new tariffs while Washington is calling the trade war “on hold.”

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but contained. The April 16 Commerce denial order showed the United States can halt a national champion overnight—ZTE stopped major operations and employs ~75,000—and the April 3 Section 301 list (~$50B, aerospace/ICT/robotics/machinery) is aimed at industrial-policy sectors, not just the trade balance. That is why the reading is above zero. It is well below the +0.5 anchor because those 301 duties are still only proposed (comment/hearing process through late May; none in force as of this date), China’s matching $50B list (soy, autos, aircraft) is also unimplemented, and the May 19 joint statement plus Mnuchin’s “on hold” line paused the cascade. Macro does not show a bite yet: industrial production still ~6.8% YoY, CPI soft, discount rate unchanged at 2.9%, reserves ~$3.13T (down <1%), CNY stronger than six months ago (~6.39 vs ~6.60). Action should be mild and slightly conciliatory, not escalatory: Liu He already framed a win as “not launching a trade war” and “stop slapping tariffs,” while Lighthizer is still reserving tariffs, investment restrictions, and export rules for structural IP issues. Escalating now would waste a pause China extracted without conceding MIC 2025 or a public $200B figure. Full purchase concessions or tariff rollback would give away chips before ZTE is actually relicensed and before 301 is formally withdrawn. Negotiate the Ross follow-up, trade volume for enforcement relief, and keep the 232 retaliation as a backstop if the hawks re-arm the 301 list.
key_factors: Section 301 $50B list still proposed, not in force
ZTE denial order remains the sharpest live threat and a bargaining chip after Trump's May 13 intervention
May 19 joint statement paused tariffs without a quantified $200B commitment or MIC 2025 rollback
Chinese real economy and FX not yet showing trade-war damage
US hawks (Lighthizer) still reserve structural tools; pause is reversible

sources_cited.excerpt: US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
USTR publishes proposed Section 301 tariff list: ~1,300 Chinese product lines (~$50B), targeting aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery and related sectors.
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods (including soybeans, automobiles, and aircraft) in response to the Section 301 list.
China imposes retaliatory tariffs on about $3B of US goods (pork, fruit, nuts, wine, and related items) in response to Section 232 steel/aluminum tariffs.
China industrial production still expanding: latest 106.8 (same period previous year = 100) as of 2018-05-01.
China reserves excluding gold ~$3.13T as of 2018-05-01, down <1% over the window — no FX-crisis signal.
CNY/USD 6.3875 on 2018-05-23 vs ~6.60 in late Nov 2017 — yuan stronger, not under depreciation stress.

Mnuchin: "We're putting the trade war on hold... we have agreed to put the tariffs on hold while we try to execute the framework." Joint statement did not specify a $200B deficit cut; Lighthizer reserved tariffs, investment restrictions and export regulations for structural IP issues.
Liu He: two sides agreed not to launch a trade war and to stop slapping tariffs against each other; structural problems will take time to resolve.
Trump tweeted he and Xi are working to get ZTE "back into business, fast"; company had halted major operating activities after the seven-year US component ban.
Section 301 tariffs will not take effect immediately; public comments due May 11, rebuttals May 22, hearing May 15.
